items.claim: An open redirect incorporates user-controllable input into a Location/href target without validating it against a trusted allowlist, enabling phishing and OAuth token/code theft.
items.body: When an application redirects to a URL taken from a request parameter or header, an attacker can craft a link that first passes through the trusted domain (borrowing its reputation) and then redirects to a malicious site. Evasions include protocol-relative URLs (//evil), backslashes, double encoding, the @-credential trick (https://target@evil), and javascript: schemes. Chaining an open redirect with OAuth makes it high-value: authorization codes and access tokens can be sent to the attacker. Prevention: never accept user-controlled redirect targets; use server-side indices; allowlist exact hosts; decode before validating; reject protocol-relative URLs and invalid schemes. CWE-601 defines the class.
items.disproof: If redirect destinations are server-mapped identifiers, or if the parsed host is compared by exact matches against an allowlisted set of trusted domains (with scheme, port, backslash, and encoded variants rejected), open redirect is neutralized. A redirect whose final Location is not within the allowlist disproves exploitation.

sources.quote: Open redirection vulnerabilities arise when an application incorporates user-controllable data into the target of a redirection in an unsafe way.
By modifying the URL value to a malicious site, an attacker may successfully launch a phishing scam. The user may be subjected to phishing attacks by being redirected to an untrusted page.
Attackers exploit open redirects mainly to bypass link-reputation filters, steal OAuth tokens, and occasionally to chain into server-side request forgery.
